did_you_know.text: Elam was an ancient kingdom in what is now southwestern Iran, while Shinar is usually associated with southern Mesopotamia. The chapter therefore describes a campaign across a great distance.
This is the first place in the Bible where the sea is called the “Salt Sea.” The Valley of Siddim is usually associated with the area around the Dead Sea.
The verb “served” does not necessarily mean personal slavery; here it can refer to political submission or paying tribute. After twelve years under that rule, the kings rebelled.
The “pits of bitumen” were places containing natural asphalt. Such deposits are indeed found in the Dead Sea region.
This is the first time the Bible calls Abraham “the Hebrew.” The word’s origin is debated: some connect it with Eber, while others link it to crossing over or coming from beyond a river.

The number 318 shows that Abraham’s household included more than his immediate family—there were also dependents born into his household. The word “trained men” may describe people prepared for their duties.
The name “Melchizedek” is usually understood as “king of righteousness.” Salem is sometimes identified with Jerusalem, though that identification is not certain.
This is the Bible’s first mention of a tithe, meaning one tenth of goods or spoils. In the ancient world, giving a tenth could be a religious practice or a payment to rulers or temples.
